prompt: Forecast next month's daily sales from three years of history with weekly and yearly seasonality.
why: Model trend and seasonality explicitly (Prophet, ETS, SARIMA).
trap: Plain regression ignores autocorrelation and seasonality.

prompt: Predict server traffic for the next 12 weeks, including the holiday peak, to plan capacity.
why: Seasonal forecasting with holiday effects and prediction intervals.
trap: Anomaly detection flags unusual traffic; it doesn't forecast it.

prompt: A utility needs hourly electricity demand for tomorrow, which depends on time of day, day of week and recent hours.
why: Lagged values plus daily and weekly seasonality: a time-series model.
trap: Treating hours as independent rows throws away the sequence.

prompt: Forecast weekly demand for 10,000 products so stores can reorder before they run out.
why: Many series forecast in parallel (often a global model with per-product history).
trap: Recommenders suggest products; they don't forecast quantities.

prompt: Forecast calls per half hour next week so the call center can schedule staff.
tells: Forecast calls per half hour next week
why: Strong daily and weekly patterns over time: a seasonal forecasting model.
trap: Anomaly detection watches for surprises; staffing needs the expected volume.

prompt: A sales forecaster looked amazing in cross-validation but failed in production. The data was randomly shuffled before splitting.
why: Shuffling leaks the future into training. Validate time series with forward-in-time splits.
trap: The model may be fine; the evaluation was wrong for sequential data.

prompt: Forecast weekly revenue, accounting for trend, Christmas peaks and a set of known upcoming promotions.
why: A forecasting model with seasonality and promotions as known future regressors.
trap: Including promotions doesn't make it a regression task; time structure still matters.

prompt: A model forecasting monthly users keeps underestimating because users grow every month. The analyst considers modeling month-over-month differences instead.
why: Differencing removes the trend so ARIMA-style models work on a stationary series.
trap: Steady growth isn't an anomaly; it's a trend to model.
